assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks (magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms, proposed by Katori) have brought fractional uncertainty and stability to the 1e-18 level and opened relativistic geodesy and tests of fundamental constants. Original idea, clean physics, and a transformative measurement capability that I can judge well from atomic-structure and polarizability-calculation perspective.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed and first realized the magic-wavelength lattice concept; Ye's group drove the experimental performance (Sr clocks, cavity-stabilized lasers, many-body/ spin-exchange control) to record accuracy. A two-person prize is natural; Hall/Hansch comb prize (2005) covers the frequency comb component, and ion clocks (Wineland 2012) are separate. Others (Lemonde, Gill, Schmidt/ion-clock groups) could be argued for.
assessment.maturity: Strong independent confirmation across many laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, SYRTE, PTB, NIST) and comparison with ion clocks; clocks are being used for redefinition of the second discussions. Recognition is timely, arguably overdue.
uncertainties: Precise division of credit between Katori's concept and the broader community (Ye, Lemonde and others) is debatable.
Whether the committee prefers a combined clock prize with other precision-metrology advances is unclear.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene revealed flat bands, correlated insulators and superconductivity in a tunable two-dimensional platform, spawning the field of moire quantum matter. Originality and impact are very high, and the conceptual simplicity of twist angle as a control parameter is striking.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald predicted the magic angle and flat bands in 2011; Jarillo-Herrero's group (with Cao, Fatemi and co-workers) discovered the correlated and superconducting states in 2018. MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero capture theory and experiment; Bistritzer is the co-author of the key theory paper and the junior-credit question is real, as are the roles of the early student-level experimentalists (Cao) who cannot be credited under this list.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced widely and extended to many moire systems, though the mechanism of superconductivity and the nature of the correlated states remain actively debated; only about eight years old, so timing is somewhat early but the field is robust.
uncertainties: Pairing mechanism in magic-angle graphene is not settled.
Credit for Bistritzer and for early experimental contributions is left out by a two-name configuration.
Possible premature timing relative to maturity of the field.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators, followed by experimental realization in HgTe quantum wells and Bi-based materials, created a new topological classification of band insulators with robust edge/surface states. Foundational and with long-lasting influence on materials physics and beyond.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the Z2 and quantum spin Hall predictions; Molenkamp's group observed the quantum spin Hall effect in HgTe wells following Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang's proposal. The list omits Zhang and others (Moore, Balents, Fu, Hasan) whose contributions are also decisive, so the configuration is contentious although the supplied three are defensible.
assessment.maturity: Extensive independent confirmation by many groups and materials; mature field, with the 2016 topological-phase prize already recognizing related ideas (Thouless, Haldane, Kosterlitz), which could argue for a degree of overlap.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2016 prize and contested credit for the 3D topological insulator versus the 2D quantum spin Hall effect.
The omitted names in the supplied credit list (e.g., Bernevig, Zhang, Hasan, Moore, Fu) complicate fairness.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices provide clean, tunable quantum simulators of Hubbard physics, with the observation of the superfluid-to-Mott transition, single-site-resolved quantum gas microscopy and fermionic Hubbard systems. High conceptual importance for many-body physics, using atomic physics to address condensed-matter questions.
assessment.attribution: Greiner, Bloch and Hansch observed the Mott transition (2002); Bloch and Greiner developed quantum gas microscopy; Esslinger pioneered fermionic lattices and Mott insulators; Zoller and Jaksch proposed the Bose-Hubbard realization. Selecting three from the list is workable but leaves out Zoller, whose proposals were seminal, and Jaksch is not on the list.
assessment.maturity: Mature and widely reproduced; the experimental platform is well-established though the scientific payoff for open problems (e.g., the fermionic Hubbard phase diagram at low temperature) is still unfolding.
uncertainties: Overlap in credit with the quantum-simulation, Rydberg-array and BEC prizes.
Whether the major payoff is a demonstrated simulation advantage that is not yet established.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum key distribution connects fundamental quantum mechanics (no-cloning, entanglement) to provably secure communication; BB84 and E91 have grown into a field and commercial and satellite demonstrations exist. Conceptually original and with significant lasting impact on quantum information science.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard authored BB84; Ekert's 1991 entanglement-based protocol is a distinct and independent contribution tied to Bell inequalities. All three have clear and separately identifiable credit, and a three-way prize is natural. Wiesner's earlier conjugate-coding idea is a notable historical precursor that this list cannot credit.
assessment.maturity: Strong experimental realization over decades and by many groups, including satellite links; the 2022 prize on entangled photons and Bell tests provides a close connection. Timing is reasonable, though practical-security loopholes remain a technology rather than a physics issue.
uncertainties: The relation to the 2022 prize and the role of Wiesner's precursor.
Practical security of implementations is an engineering question separate from the physics merit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit quantum electrodynamics, with strong coupling of a superconducting qubit to a microwave resonator, established the architecture underlying present superconducting quantum processors and a platform for quantum optics on a chip. Original and widely adopted, with a direct link to my own interest in light-matter interaction.
assessment.attribution: Blais, Huang, Wallraff, Girvin and Schoelkopf (2004) proposed and demonstrated strong coupling in cQED; Girvin cannot be included in a three-person configuration if Schoelkopf, Wallraff and Blais are taken, creating a real allocation problem among four names. Wallraff and Schoelkopf led the experiments; Blais and Girvin led the theory.
assessment.maturity: Very well confirmed across laboratories; the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits is closely related and recent, so recognition of cQED soon after could be seen as premature, or as a natural sequel.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2025 prize and difficulty of a three-person limit given four credited names.
Whether Girvin should replace Blais is not resolved.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Squeezed-light injection beyond the standard quantum limit, proposed by Caves and demonstrated in the lab and in gravitational-wave interferometers, is a clean application of quantum optics to real precision measurement and extends the reach of LIGO and Virgo.
assessment.attribution: Caves provided the theoretical proposal (1981); Kimble's early squeezing experiments (with Slusher's group at Bell Labs also relevant but not credited); Schnabel and Mavalvala drove the GW-detector implementation. The four-name list means a difficult three-person choice, and Slusher is not on the list.
assessment.maturity: Operational use in LIGO and GEO600 is a strong independent demonstration; the concept is mature but the prize should reflect which part of the chain is decisive.
uncertainties: Dividing credit between concept, early experiments and detector implementation is difficult.
Kimble is omitted in this configuration and has strong claims.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Programmable arrays of Rydberg-interacting neutral atoms bring atomic physics to quantum simulation and computation, with Rydberg blockade, optical-tweezer arrays and programmable many-body states. Important and fast-moving, and the relevant atomic-structure physics is something I understand well.
assessment.attribution: Saffman and Lukin developed Rydberg blockade-based gate proposals; Browaeys and Lukin led the experimental array simulators; Jaksch and Zoller proposed the original fast Rydberg gate, which is not credited here. The decisive contributors are diffuse and the allocation is unresolved.
assessment.maturity: Rapidly maturing with independent groups reproducing results, but the long-term significance (error-corrected computation or new many-body phases) is not yet settled, so timing may be early.
uncertainties: Credit for the original Rydberg gate proposals not on this list.
Premature relative to the final value as a quantum computing platform.
